output.methodChoice: Kepner-Tregoe specification/distinctions (gap by eligibility), then ACH across hypotheses, with evidence-ledger provenance check on the COO's stake
output.brief: The promotion gap is mostly a tenure effect, not proof of proximity bias. Remote work was opened to all roles only in July 2024, so 230 of 340 remote staff (68%) have under 18 months in level and are ineligible under policy, against 26% of office staff. Among eligible people, nomination rates (28.2% vs 28.6%), approval rates (71% vs 74%) and promotion rates (20.0% vs 21.1%) are nearly the same. Applying office rates to the remote tenure mix predicts 8.2% remote, against 7.6% observed. Remote staff don't leave more often (10.9% vs 11.6%), and the gap shows in every job family, so job mix doesn't explain it. Caveat: only 110 remote staff are eligible, so a real difference of a few points can't be ruled out. The interview and survey hints about uneven stretch work and less clarity on promotion criteria remain unverified. Recommendation: don't adopt the three-day office rule. It would exclude about 180 people hired on home-based contracts, and the evidence doesn't support it. Hold it, report promotion rates for eligible staff only, and re-check at FY2027. Separately, check how stretch assignments are distributed, and consider briefing staff on promotion criteria. Confidence is fairly high on the main finding.
